note: The 'Why?' cards: after each reveal, one card names the specific cause. Every sentence a player reads is a template in this file with named placeholders filled in. js/why.js substitutes values and never composes a sentence, so the card cannot say anything that is not written here. docs/PRD.md: 'template text cannot invent wrong answers'.
placeholderNote: {r} is a correlation, shown to 2 decimals, or to 4 when it sits within 0.005 of the level's own pass threshold, so the card and the reveal panel can never show the same number differently. {riskPct} and {dollarPct} are whole percents. No template states the gap between two percents as its own number: rounding each to a whole percent can make a 15-point gap read as 14 or 16, and a number that disagrees with the two beside it is worse than no number.
levelOneNote: Level 1 asks for two holdings and no money split, so the risk-share rules below would describe a split the player never chose. It gets a correlation card instead: one template for each 'Same bet?' bucket in levels.json, keyed by that file's own bucket keys. A test holds the two files to each other.

same.template: {a} and {b} move together almost every day, at {r}. Two different names, and very nearly the same bet.

partly.says: the pair moves together some of the time
partly.template: {a} and {b} move together some of the time, at {r}. Partly the same bet: they share some of what drives them, but not all of it.

different.says: the pair moves on different things
different.template: {a} and {b} move on different things, at {r}. Knowing what one did on a given day tells you little about the other, so these are two real bets.

leadIn.note: One line before the card, on the levels that have a portfolio to pass or miss. It is a separate template from the card, rendered as its own line, and the two are never joined into one sentence: that is what keeps 'no generated prose' true with two templates on screen.
leadIn.levelsNote: Levels 2 and 3 only. Level 1's bucket cards carry no lead-in: its own reveal panel already says whether the pair cleared 0.80, and the bucket line under it says which bucket the guess named, so a third verdict line would be the same news a third time.
leadIn.pathNote: Which pair of lines a level uses depends on what its pass rule measures. A level that checks the PORTFOLIO - level 3's 'at least 3 effective bets' - gets passed or missed. A level whose pass rule IS the guess - level 2's 'make a guess', which every round satisfies - has no portfolio to pass or miss, so its line speaks to the guess instead: there is no verdict on the build to report, and 'You passed' on a level nobody can fail says nothing.
leadIn.closeNote: Close means the round earned the level's own two-star band, which levels.json words for level 2 as 'within 1 bet'. The band is read from levels.json rather than repeated here on purpose: the line sits directly under the stars it describes, and a second copy of the number could drift from the first and have the screen contradict itself.
leadIn.passed: You passed. One thing to notice:
leadIn.closeGuess: Close guess. One thing to notice:
leadIn.wideGuess: Here's what made this one tricky:

orderNote: The first rule in this list whose test passes is the card that gets shown. One card, not a list: on a phone, one cause a player can carry away beats three they skim. hiddenAi answers first because the exposure it names is the one a player cannot see on their own screen - the AI inside a fund they chose for being broad - and its own conditions stand it down whenever the AI is held in the open, where the group card says it better. Group concentration comes next because it is the fullest version of the lesson: five AI stocks is both 'your closest pair moves together' and 'one group holds the risk', and the second says more. fewBets comes after it and before pair, which is the placement that lets it win on four funds that each carry a quarter of the risk and still make one bet: the top group holds about half, so groupRisk is silent, and the 0.99 pair inside it would otherwise take the card and say the smaller thing. The risk-gap rules come last because they are about the split rather than about what a player picked.

rules.says: a fund is carrying all of the AI exposure
rules.whenNote: The same card as hiddenAi for the case where the fund accounts for the WHOLE beta, which on level 4 is the ordinary way to pass rather than an edge case: QQQ at its floor beside bonds and staples, several of which move slightly against the basket, so what they take off cancels what gold and the broad fund add. It fires when the fund's part of the beta is at least the whole of it, or rounds to the whole of it at the two decimals the card prints. It sits directly before hiddenAi in the order, and the two are exact complements: every portfolio one of them would speak to is spoken to by exactly one of them.
rules.wordingNote: Without this, the card read 'Your portfolio moves 0.17% when AI stocks move 1%, and 0.17 of that comes from QQQ alone' - true, and it reads as a typo. Found by playing level 4 in a browser, not by a test: both numbers were right.
rules.template: Your portfolio moves {portfolioBeta}% when AI stocks move 1%, and all of that comes from {ticker} alone, which is only {dollarPct} of your money. The AI is inside the fund.

rules.says: a fund is carrying the AI exposure
rules.whenNote: Three conditions, and each one has to hold for the sentence to be true of this portfolio. portfolioBetaAtLeast keeps the card off a portfolio that barely moves with the basket at all, where a part of a beta near zero means nothing. shareOfBetaAtLeast asks that the one holding brings at least half of what there is. fundGroups is the one that stops the card lying: 'The AI is inside the fund' is false of a chipmaker, and INTC is not in basket.json but carries a beta of about 1.0 to it, so without this the card would name INTC and call it a fund.
rules.unitsNote: Both numbers are betas, never shares of a beta. JNJ, PG, KO and XOM all move slightly AGAINST the AI basket, so a holding's share of the total can run past 100% and below 0%: QQQ beside staples comes to 148% of its own portfolio's beta. {portfolioBeta} is how far the portfolio moves when the basket moves 1%, and {contribution} is how much of that one holding brings.
rules.template: Your portfolio moves {portfolioBeta}% when AI stocks move 1%, and {contribution} of that comes from {ticker} alone, which is only {dollarPct} of your money. The AI is inside the fund.

rules.says: one group holds most of the risk
rules.whenNote: Below 3 holdings, 'one group holds most of the risk' is true by arithmetic and teaches nothing: two Core US funds are 100% of their own risk. That is why minHoldings is 3.
rules.minGroupsNote: minGroups was 2 in the first draft, to keep the card off a portfolio that is all one group. That was wrong, and a browser check caught it: five AI stocks make 1.03 bets, the lesson this whole game is named after, and the card read 'nothing stands out here'. A portfolio that is ALL one group is the most concentrated one a player can build, not the least worth mentioning. The case the guard was written for - two holdings from one group - is level 1, and level 1 takes the bucket path and never reaches these rules at all.
rules.thresholdNote: 70% of the risk, chosen on real prices rather than guessed. At the 50% first drafted, this card won 73% of 420 test portfolios - a player would read very nearly the same sentence every round, and 'most of the risk' is a weak claim when a 5-holding portfolio spans only two or three groups. At 70% it wins 38%, and the claim is one a player can see in the numbers. BUILD_LOG.md carries the table.
rules.template: {count} of your {total} holdings are {group}. They are {dollarPct} of your money and {riskPct} of your risk, so that is where this portfolio's fortunes are decided - and where the damage lands on a bad day.
rules.templateNote: The tail has to read as well at 100% as at 71%, because a portfolio that is all one group now reaches this card. An earlier draft ended 'they are doing most of the work', which understates it when the answer is all of it.
rules.minHoldingsInGroupNote: A group of ONE holding is not a group, it is a holding. Without this, three bond funds beside NVDA read '1 of your 4 holdings are AI stocks. They are 25% of your money and 82% of your risk' - bad grammar, and a weaker claim than the truth, which is that one holding carries four fifths of the risk. riskGapOver already has the template for that, so a one-holding group falls through to it. Found by the lesson portfolio added for level 5's failing build, which is the first case in the set where a single holding dominates a 3-or-more-holding portfolio.

rules.says: the risk is spread evenly and it is still one bet
rules.thresholdNote: 2.00 bets, derived rather than tuned: with 4 holdings it is the claim that four collapsed to fewer than two, which a player can check against the number the reveal panel just showed them. It also sits below level 3's own 3-bet bar, so nothing this card calls mostly one bet is a portfolio the game elsewhere calls diversified. Measured on the frozen snapshot: of 2,000 seeded 4-holding builds, the 213 that pass level 5 have a median of 1.31 bets, and 92% of them are under 2.00. At 1.50 it would catch 69% of them and at 2.25, 97%. BUILD_LOG.md session 2.5 carries the table.
rules.whenNote: maxRiskShareBelow is level 5's own pass threshold, so 'the risk is spread' means the same thing on the card as it does in the level that checks it. minHoldings is groupRisk's guard, for the same reason: with two holdings, evenly spread risk and one bet is arithmetic rather than a lesson.
rules.template: No holding carries more than {maxRiskPct} of the risk, yet your {total} holdings make only {bets} separate bets. The risk is spread evenly, but it's still mostly one bet, because these holdings move together.

rules.thresholdNote: The correlation was left where it was after the real-data check: moving it only trades this card against the fallback, and one number meaning one thing across the whole game is worth more than a balanced table.
rules.pairRiskNote: pairRiskAtLeast asks that the two holdings carry at least a fifth of the portfolio's risk between them. Without it the card could name two bond funds correlated 0.94 that are 5% of what moves the portfolio - a true sentence about a corner of it, crowding out what is actually driving the number. 20% was measured: it removes 10 of the 76 pair cards in the 420-portfolio check, every one of them a pair under a fifth of the risk. Going higher gets expensive fast - at 35% the rule loses 49 of 76, including VEA and VXUS at 0.99, two funds that are nearly the same fund, which is the clearest statement of this whole game's lesson. The pair that carries little risk is not dropped; it falls to pairLowRisk below.
rules.whenNote: 0.70 is the 'same bet' edge already used by levels.json's buckets and by the daily 'Same bet?' puzzle, so one number means one thing across the whole game.
rules.template: {a} and {b} are the closest pair you hold, at {r}. They rise and fall together, so the two of them count as closer to one bet than two.

rules.says: a holding's share of risk is far bigger than its share of money
rules.whenNote: 20 points of the portfolio. Below that the two percents read as near enough the same, and the card would be making a point out of rounding.
rules.thresholdNote: Raised from the 15 first drafted after the real-data check: at 15 points this rule had something to say about three quarters of all portfolios, which is too loose to be called a gap.
rules.template: {ticker} is {dollarPct} of your money but {riskPct} of your risk. Share of risk is not share of dollars: a holding that swings harder than the rest carries more of the risk than its size suggests.

rules.says: a pair that moves together but carries little of the risk
rules.whenNote: The exact complement of the pair rule's own risk condition: pairRiskBelow here and pairRiskAtLeast there must be the same number, or a pair would fall between the two rules and get no card at all. A test holds them equal, and holds the two correlation thresholds equal too.
rules.template: {a} and {b} move together, at {r}, but between them they are only {riskPct} of your risk. They are the same bet - just not the bet that decided this portfolio.

rules.says: a holding's share of money is far bigger than its share of risk
rules.thresholdNote: 15 points, deliberately lower than riskGapOver's 20, and the asymmetry is structural rather than a preference. The shares sum to 1, so the gaps sum to 0: a holding 20 points under its dollar share means other holdings are over, and riskGapOver takes them first. Held to the same 20 this card never appeared at all in 420 test portfolios. At 15 it appears in 7%.
rules.whenNote: The same 15 points, the other way round. riskShareAtLeast keeps the card off a holding whose share of risk is negative, which happens when a holding offsets the rest rather than adding to it: that is a real thing a portfolio can do, but it is a different lesson from steadiness and has no template of its own. This is the bond-fund case, and it is a separate template rather than a reworded one, because the lesson is the opposite: steadiness, not concentration.
rules.template: {ticker} is {dollarPct} of your money but only {riskPct} of your risk. It moves more quietly than the rest, so it takes up room in the portfolio without adding much to what can go wrong.

rulesTail: pairLowRisk is the pair card demoted rather than dropped. A pair correlated 0.70 or more that carries less than a fifth of the risk is still the same bet, and still worth naming - but it is not what decided the number, and it says so. It sits LAST in the order on purpose: if it ran before the risk-gap rules it would simply hand back the cards pairRiskAtLeast took away, and the condition would have been for nothing. Last means it speaks only when nothing else had anything to say.

fallback.template: Nothing stands out here. No pair you hold moves closely together, no holding carries much more risk than money, and no one group holds most of the risk. That is what a spread-out portfolio looks like from the inside.
